dossier.public_summary: The 0.66-day dip lands on the star but matches the star's 0.66-day rotation exactly and shows a huge brightness swing outside the dips. Its depth triples from 7,500 to 22,860 ppm and individual dips vary wildly, which planets do not. Together this is stellar variability, not a planet.

reasons.why: Huge out-of-dip modulation comparable to the transit depth, best explained by ellipsoidal/spotted stellar variability at this period, not a planet.
Dip period is essentially the stellar rotation period (multiple =1) with very high spot amplitudes, so the dip co-phases with rotation.
reasons.value: rotation_d 0.659 signal_period_d 0.659756 signal_over_rotation 1.0011471927162368 amplitude_ppm up to 51714

reasons.why: Depth more than triples between sectors; sector_depths_by_source = changes_within_a_source (SPOC 2-min p_constant 6.102732756224227e-27, TESS-SPOC p_constant 1.2370428860652167e-11). A planet should be steady, this is not.
reasons.value: p_constant 3.641e-40 depth_change_pct 97.22 per-sector 7494, 12191, 20677, 22860 ppm chi2 186.4 dof 3

reasons.why: Individual transit depths are highly inconsistent, as expected for starspots/systematics, not a stable transit.
Duration is much too long for central transit on this 0.546 Rsun M dwarf and the light curve requires extreme impact parameter/density mismatch, favours no planet.
Independent classifier rates as strongly planet-unlike, consistent with the above false-positive signs.
